A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Cross-domain Integrated Gradients work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support comparison, including matching material moved or renumbered in v2.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic CNN experiments and attribution results for heart-rate extraction, EEG seizure detection, and TimesFM forecasting.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds insertion/deletion evaluations in Tables 1–2 and additional attribution examples in Appendices G–H.

M1.justification: The attribution definition, complex-gradient construction, inverse-transform procedure, and Algorithms 1–3 are retained. New remarks about alternative integration paths and filtered-component baselines discuss possibilities without establishing an implemented method change.

E1.justification: The real datasets and application tasks remain unchanged. Synthetic forecasting coverage expands modestly: v1 uses a fixed exponential-trend parameter of 4 and base frequency of 2 Hz, while v2 adds examples with parameters sampled from 4–7 and 3–8 Hz, respectively (Appendix J).

E2.justification: Comparison participation expands beyond v1's synthetic time-versus-frequency IG example. v2 Table 1 compares Frequency IG with Time IG and random frequency selection; Table 2 compares ICA IG with random component selection. Appendix G also adds time-domain IG comparisons for all three applications.

E3.justification: Appendix F introduces substantial new evaluation protocols: HR insertion/deletion at 3.125%, 25%, and 50% of features, with prediction distances averaged across 15 subjects; and EEG interventions on one component using the first seizure-detected sample per session. Appendix J specifies randomized parameters for additional forecasting examples.

E4.justification: v2 adds feature insertion/deletion analyses testing attribution sufficiency and necessity, direct time-domain attribution examples, and additional application case studies (Appendices F–H). The frequency-response probe already present in v1 Figure 2 is retained as v2 Figure 5, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or statistical uncertainty estimates. Averaging the new HR results across 15 subjects does not introduce repeated-run or uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v2 adds Tables 1–2 and numerous attribution outputs. For example, Table 1 reports 3.125% deletion distances of 66.39, 10.13, and 8.53 BPM for Frequency IG, Time IG, and Random, respectively, with no v1 counterpart. The original HR errors of 0.93/26.78 BPM and forecasting errors of 0.2/2.14 remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix D adds a special-case derivation claiming DFT equivalence to Virtual Inspection Layers, and Remark 1 discusses general integration paths. The core definition, lemma proof, and CNN derivation are retained or relocated. The new derivation contains an unexplained loss of the normalization factor between Equations 19 and 20.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same method, complex-domain extension, applications, and library claims. The introduction newly makes explicit claims of Sensitivity and Implementation Invariance alongside Completeness, modestly expanding the stated theoretical guarantees.

C2.justification: v2 interprets insertion/deletion results as evidence of more faithful, concentrated component attributions and explains why mixed signal sources complicate time-point interpretation. It also discusses inverse-transform overhead, filtered-component baselines, and combined or automatic domain selection. Most original application interpretations and limitations remain.

D1.justification: Appendices F and J document intervention selection rules and synthetic parameter distributions for the added experiments. Existing FastICA hyperparameters, 512-point input and 128-step forecast lengths, V100 hardware disclosure, and code-access information are retained.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning around saliency evaluation, adding discussion and citations concerning benchmarks, evaluation ambiguity, and insertion/deletion tests. More significantly, Appendix D claims equivalence to Vielhaben et al.'s Virtual Inspection Layers for DFT attribution, whereas v1 only contrasted that work's transform-specific relevance rules with the proposed generalization.

P1.justification: v2 substantially reorganizes the narrative: Methods gains numbered subsections, detailed proofs move to Appendices B–C, and applications are rewritten around explicit interpretability tasks, transformations, and numbered remarks. It also adds an evaluation overview and separates the ethical statement from the relocated limitations.

P2.justification: v2 adds two evaluation tables and seven figures covering interventions, time-domain attributions, and additional application examples. Existing application figures are retained and renumbered, while the frequency-response figure moves from the main text to Appendix E. These materially expand and reorganize the visual presentation.

improvement.justification: Compared with v1's largely illustrative application evidence, v2 supplies quantitative intervention comparisons and clearer explanations of how to use the unchanged method. These strengthen empirical support and readability. However, the seizure metric's sign convention is unclear, Appendix F claims tests for three applications but reports only two, and the new DFT derivation has a normalization inconsistency. These reporting problems limit the overall gain.
